To cause (a bell) to sound wit gle strokes slowly and regularly repeated, summoning public bodies or religious co gations to their meetings, for announc death, or to give solemnity to a funeral cifically, to ring (a bell) by striking it hammer without swinging.

{{smaller block|To ''Toll'' a Bell, which is to make him strike onel side.

{{smaller block|A bell of very moderate weight will soon pull nary wall to pieces if rung in full swing across i bells in "bell gables" can hardly ever be safely r that reason, but only ''tolled''.

{{smaller block|And bells ''toll'd'' out their mighty peal,

{{smaller block|Clear and loud

{{right|''Wordsworth'', Influence of Natural}}}}

{{smaller block|A sullen bell,

{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., i}}}}

{{smaller block|One set slow bell will seem to ''toll''
The passing of the sweetest soul

{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memori}}}}

'''toll-bait''' (tōl′bāt), ''n.'' Minced or chopped bait thrown overboard to toll, lure, or attract fish; gurry-bait; tollings. {{smaller|It is usually chum or stosh, and is often salted to keep until wanted for use. The process of using toll-bait is often called ''chumming'' or ''chumming up.'' Also ''throw-bait.''}}

{{smaller block|In the old style mackerel fishing, however, clams were chopped up (often with a mixture of menhaden) and sprinkled overboard as ''toll-bait'' to attract the mackerel to the surface.
{{right|''Fisheries of U. S.'', V. ii. 594.}}}}

'''toll-bar''' (tōl′bär), ''n.'' A bar or beam, or (now usually) a gate, thrown across a road or other passage at a tollhouse, for the purpose of preventing passengers, vehicles, cattle, etc., from passing without payment of toll; a turnpike. [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.]

{{smaller block|It would often be nearly 1 o'clock {{sc|a. m.}} before we reached the Newington ''toll-bar,'' which was our general point of separation.
{{right|''Harper's Mag.'', LXXX. 448.}}}}

'''toll-book''' (tōl′bu̇k), ''n.'' A book in which horses, cattle, and goods to be sold at a fair were entered for payment of tolls.

{{smaller block|Some that were Maides
E'en at Sun set, are now perhaps i' th' ''Toale-booke.''
{{right|''C. Tourneur'', Revenger's Tragedy, ii. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|Petre wente aȝen to fishing, but Mathew not to his ''tolrie.''
{{right|''Wyclif'', Select Works (ed. Arnold), II. 138.}}}}

'''Tolletan''' (tol′e-tan), ''a.'' [ME. ''Tolletane'', < L. ''Toletanus'', pertaining to ''Toletum'', < ''Toletum'', a town in Spain, now ''Toledo''.] Of or pertaining to Toledo.—{{smaller|'''Tolletan tables''', same as ''Alphonsine tables'' (which see, under ''Alphonsine''): so called as being adapted to the city of Toledo. Also ''tables Toletanes''.}}

{{smaller block|His ''tables Tolletanes'' forth he brought
Ful wel corrected, ne ther lakked nought.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Franklin's Tale, l. 545.}}}}

'''toll-free''' (tōl′frē), ''a.'' Free from the obligation of paying toll or duty.

{{smaller block|A remission of the feefarm of their city to the extent of 50''l.'' a year, in order that all persons visiting York might be made ''toll-free.''
{{right|''J. Gairdner'', Richard III., ii.}}}}

{{smaller block|Behould the Teeth, which ''Toul-free'' grinde the food,
From whence themselues do reap more grief then good.
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas's Weeks, i. 7.}}}}

'''toll-gate''' (tōl′gāt), ''n.'' A gate where toll is taken; a toll-bar.

{{smaller block|It afforded a southern stranger a new kind of pleasure to travel so commodiously without the interruption of ''toll-gates.''
{{right|''Johnson'', Journey to Western Islands (Works, VIII. 211).}}}}

'''toll-gatherer''' (tōl′gaᴛ̵ʜ″ėr-ėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''tolgadere''; < ''toll''<sup>1</sup> + ''gatherer''.] One who collects tolls or duties.

{{smaller block|Matheu, that was of Judee, . . . fro the office of a ''tolgaderer'' . . . was clepid to God.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Prol. to Mat.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Toll-gatherers'' are ever ready to search and exact sound tribute.

{{smaller block|Our Sauyor Crist goyng by sawe the publycan named Leui, otherwyse Mathew, syttynge at the ''tolhous''.

May not this person have been connected with the ''tolhouse'' or "tolbooth" (as our town halls were called in the Middle Ages)? In this place [Great Yarmouth] the name of ''tolhouse'' is still retained [1889].
{{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., VIII. 213.}}}}

2. A house placed on or beside a road near a toll-gate, or at the end of a toll-bridge, where the toll-taker is stationed.

'''tolling'''<sup>1</sup> (tō′ling), ''n.'' [Also ''toling''; verbal n. of ''toll''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.''] 1. The use of toll-bait to attract fish; the practice or method of drawing fish, as a school of mackerel, by means of gurry, chum, or stosh thrown overboard. The tolling is done by one of a crew while the others fish.—2. ''pl.'' Toll-bait.—3. A method of decoying or luring ducks. See the quotation. [U. S.]

{{smaller block|The system pursued on the Chesapeake Bay and the North Carolina Sounds, and known as ''toling'', is the most successful. It is as follows: A small dog, an ordinary poodle, or one very much similar to that, white or brown in color, and called the toler breed, is kept for the purpose. It is trained to run up and down on the shore in the sight of the ducks, directed by the motion of his owner's hand. The curiosity of the ducks is excited, and they approach the shore to discover the nature of the object which has attracted their attention. They raise their heads, look intently, and then start in a body for the shore.
{{right|''Dogs of Great Britain and America'', p. 271.}}}}

'''tolling'''<sup>2</sup> (tō′ling), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''toling''; verbal n. of ''toll''<sup>3</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' The act of sounding a bell. See ''toll''<sup>3</sup>.—'''2.''' The sound produced by a bell under single measured strokes of the clapper.

{{smaller block|It [the campanero] is especially celebrated for its extraordinary voice, which is compared with the ''tolling'' of a bell.
{{right|''Stand. Nat. Hist.'', IV. 475.}}}}

{{smaller block|The great superiority of tone of bells ringing in full swing over ''tolling'', and even of ''tolling'' over striking by a clock hammer, has been often noticed.
{{right|''Sir E. Beckett'', Clocks, Watches, and Bells, p. 373.}}}}

'''3.''' A peculiar bell-like sound said to be made by bees before they swarm. [Scotch.]

{{smaller block|Most observers also affirm that in the evening before swarming an uncommon humming or buzzing is heard in the hive, and a distinct sound from the queen, called ''tolling'' or calling. Mr. Hunter compares it to the notes of a pianoforte.
{{right|''Edin. Encyc.'', art. Bee, quoted in Jamieson.}}}}

'''tolling-lever''' (tō′ling-lev″ėr), ''n.'' A lever or shank projecting from the top of the clapper, and pulled by means of a light rope, to sound the bell. {{smaller|It is designed to save the heavy swinging of the bell in a weak tower. ''Sir E. Beckett'', Clocks, Watches,}} and Bells, p. 371.
